anchors.text: Well, the park I visit the most is a riverside park about ten minutes from my place. Honestly it's my favorite spot because it really helps me relax after a long day. It's long and narrow because it follows the river, and there's a bike path, some benches, and a lot of tall trees on both sides. In the spring there are cherry blossoms everywhere, so it gets really crowded. I usually go there in the evening after work. I walk along the river and listen to podcasts, and sometimes I meet my friend there and we grab a coffee from a convenience store. When the sun goes down the river looks really beautiful, so I just sit on a bench and watch it. I think going there is the best way to clear my head.

anchors.text: Okay, so the park I go to most often is Seoul Forest, and honestly it's kind of my escape from the city because whenever I'm there I feel like I can finally breathe. It's a huge park right next to the Han River, and what I love about it is that it has so many different areas. There's a big open lawn where people lie down on mats, there's a little deer enclosure, which is pretty unusual for a park in the middle of Seoul, and there are these long walking trails surrounded by really tall trees. In the summer the trees make a lot of shade so it doesn't feel that hot. I usually go there on Sunday mornings when it's still quiet. I grab an iced americano, walk around for about an hour, and then I just sit on the grass and read. Last month I went there with my sister and we had a picnic, and we ended up staying until the sun went down. It was, you know, one of those days that remind me why I love this place so much.

anchors.text: The park I find myself going back to again and again is Olympic Park in the southeast of Seoul, and honestly it's the one place where I can completely switch off, because the moment I walk in the noise of the city just kind of fades away. It's enormous, so it never feels crowded even on weekends. Right at the entrance there's a wide plaza with a huge gate, and once you pass it you see these gentle grassy hills that roll all the way to the horizon. My favorite spot is a single tree standing alone on a hill. People call it the lonely tree, and it's become kind of a landmark for photographers. When I was in college I used to go there to study for exams, because sitting under that tree somehow made me focus better than any library. These days I mostly go there to run. I'll do a lap around the park, which takes about forty minutes, and by the time I'm done I feel like I've reset my whole week. If I ever moved out of Seoul, I think that park is honestly the thing I would miss the most.

anchors.text: The most memorable trip I took with my family was to Jeju Island three years ago, and I still remember it because it was our last trip before my older brother went to the army. We stayed there for four days in the summer. On the first day we went to Hyeopjae beach. The water was so clear that you could see the sand under it, and we just swam and played in the water all afternoon. The next day we decided to climb Hallasan. It took almost five hours and my mom wanted to give up in the middle, but we encouraged her and finally we reached the top together. Everybody was exhausted but really proud. That night we had black pork barbecue and talked until late. Whenever I see the pictures from that trip, I feel a little emotional because we don't have many chances like that anymore.

anchors.text: The trip I remember the most is the one we took to Jeju Island three summers ago, mainly because it was the last time all four of us traveled together before my brother joined the army. So, um, we rented a car and drove around the island for four days. The first day was pretty relaxed, we just went to Hyeopjae beach, which has this amazing emerald water, and we spent the whole afternoon swimming. But the highlight was definitely the second day when we climbed Hallasan. We started at like six in the morning and honestly it was much harder than we expected. Halfway up, my mom said she couldn't go any further, and for a moment we thought we should turn back. But my brother carried her backpack and we kind of cheered her on, and after almost five hours we made it to the crater lake at the top. I'll never forget my mom's face when she saw the view. Looking back, I think that moment brought us closer as a family, and now that my brother is busy with his own life, I really treasure that memory.

anchors.text: If I had to pick one trip, it would definitely be the one my family took to Jeju Island three summers ago, and the reason it stands out is that, without anyone saying it out loud, we all knew it was probably the last time the four of us would travel together for a long while, since my brother was about to enlist. We rented a car and spent four days circling the island. The first couple of days were pretty laid back. We spent hours at Hyeopjae beach, where the water is this unreal shade of emerald, and in the evenings we wandered around the local markets trying everything from tangerine chocolate to grilled hairtail. What really made the trip, though, was our hike up Hallasan. We set off before sunrise, and about halfway up my mom told us she simply couldn't keep going. My brother, who had barely spoken all morning, quietly took her backpack and walked beside her for the rest of the climb. When we finally reached the crater lake at the summit, my mom burst into tears, and honestly so did I. Now that my brother has moved to another city and we rarely see each other, I've realized that those few hours on the mountain are what I think of whenever someone mentions the word family.

anchors.text: There are a few environmental issues in Korea. The biggest one is fine dust. Especially in spring, the air quality is really bad and sometimes you can't even see the buildings far away. So many people check the air quality app every morning and wear masks when they go outside. Another issue is plastic waste. People use a lot of plastic cups and delivery containers. To solve this problem, the government made rules about recycling, and people have to separate their trash very carefully. Also some cafes don't give plastic cups inside the store anymore. I think these efforts are good but we need to do more.

anchors.text: I think the most serious environmental problem in Korea is fine dust. Every spring, the sky turns kind of yellow and gray, and on bad days the government sends emergency text messages telling people to stay inside. A lot of the dust comes from factories and cars, and some of it also comes from other countries, so it's not easy to solve. People usually deal with it by wearing masks and using air purifiers at home. The second big issue is plastic waste, especially because of food delivery. When I order food, I get so many plastic containers that I feel guilty. Korea has pretty strict recycling rules, so people sort their trash into different bins, and recently some cafes started using reusable cups. Personally I try to bring my own tumbler, but honestly I think companies need to change more than individuals.

anchors.text: Well, I'd say the two biggest environmental issues in Korea right now are air pollution, especially fine dust, and plastic waste. Fine dust has become a part of everyday life here. When I was a kid, I don't remember anyone talking about it, but now almost everyone checks the air quality forecast before leaving the house, and on really bad days schools even cancel outdoor activities. The causes are complicated. Part of it is coal power plants and diesel cars here, and part of it blows over from neighboring countries, so the government has been trying things like limiting old diesel cars in Seoul and temporarily shutting down some coal plants in spring. As for plastic, the delivery culture has made it much worse, especially during the pandemic when everyone was ordering in. People here are actually pretty good at recycling because the rules are strict, but the problem is that a lot of it can't really be recycled. Personally, I think recycling alone isn't enough, and companies should be pushed to reduce packaging in the first place.

anchors.text: When people talk about the environment in Korea, the first thing that usually comes up is fine dust, and I think that's fair, because it's the one issue that affects everyone's daily life in a very visible way. On a bad day the sky turns this hazy yellow, you get an emergency alert on your phone, and suddenly half the people on the subway are wearing masks. What makes it so frustrating is that the causes are tangled together. Domestic factors like coal-fired power plants and diesel vehicles play a big role, but a significant share drifts in from abroad, so no single policy can fix it. The government has responded with a mix of measures, from restricting older diesel cars in Seoul to scaling back coal plants during the spring. The other issue I'd point to is plastic waste, which has quietly grown because of how convenient delivery culture has become. Ironically, Korea is known for having one of the strictest recycling systems in the world, yet a lot of what we carefully separate ends up being incinerated because it's contaminated or made of mixed materials. So in my view, the real solution isn't asking individuals to recycle even harder, but requiring companies to redesign their packaging so that less waste is produced in the first place.
